description:
What is LOCUST BEAN GUM? The ice cream stabilizer series talks about these special ingredients you NEED to know about if you keep your ice cream for longer than a week. 

As part of the ice cream stabilizer series here on Polar Ice Creamery, the next one to discus is Locust Bean gum. It is often shortened to LBG in recipes and is a really useful stabilizer. 

Used in a miriad of recipes, food stuffs, cosmetics etc the list again is endless. Made from the seeds of the Locust Bean Tree (Parkia biglobosa), the seed pods are dried, the seeds removed and then roasted before finally being ground down to fine off white powder. 

Ususally you use LBG with another stabilizer such as Guar Gum as on it's own, it can result in Wheying off. This is when the whey seeps out of your ice cream when melting in a bowl. To combat this, the partner stabilizers, stop this happening. 

Ice cream stabilizers are a complex subject as there are a lot of different ones that all create a part of a larger puzzle. When done right, a properly stabilized ice cream stands head and shoulders above the rest. 

Next week, I will be talking about Carrageenans, there are three different ones and each should be used i different ways. So if you want to find out more about this complex subject, click the subscribe button and I'll see you next time.

comments.text:
No, there are no real insects (locusts) in locust bean gum. It is a 100% plant-based, vegan thickening agent derived from the seeds of the carob tree (Ceratonia siliqua), which grows in the Mediterranean. The name comes from the carob pods' resemblance to the insect, not from the insect itself. 
Source: The gum is derived from the endosperm of carob seeds.
Production: The seeds are processed to remove the tough brown seed coat (husk) and the germ, leaving the inner white endosperm, which is ground into a fine powder.
Uses: It is widely used as a stabilizer, thickener, and emulsifier in dairy products, desserts, and sauces.
Synonyms: It is sometimes called Carob Bean Gum or E410.

comments.text: Can I use locust beam gum to thicken yogurt?  Does it change the taste?  If so, do I incorporate the locust bean gum while denaturing the milk? What percentage should I use?  Thank you

comments.text: If it’s just plain yogurt then you’d probably be better off using Xanthan or guar gum to thicken it. Neither have a taste and that’s what they are designed to do, Locust bean gum is not the right ingredient for that purpose.

comments.text: Thank you so much for all your great work ❤ I love your videos and even more your recipes. Completely upped my ice cream game 🎉. A question about stabilisers: how do you store them? (Cool dark place, ok, but maybe freezer is better?) Do you know if they go rancid? Assuming I'm not the kind of person who fears due date. LBG was so expensive but it'll take me forever to use it up, I wouldn't want it to spoil...
comments.author: @shvekal

comments.text:
Light or dark doesn’t make a difference, humidity is the issue. If you can keep the powders dry, they’ll last indefinitely. I have a tub of pre-mix stabilizer that’s over a year old. I also have an opened bag of LBG which I put a good grade silica pouch in, it’s still perfectly dry after 2 years. 
The dates don’t mean much for stabilizers really, most food items spoil due to to too much moisture. Thankfully, I’m pretty well trained on moisture and it’s effects on food.
